In putting this motion
to the House I may state that I have examined the question during the past few days and while I have come to a decision as to its right to be on the order paper, I should like to have an expression of opinion from the House on that point. In my judgment the motion is out of order, inasmuch as the question at issue is sub judice; it is a matter which at present is pending before the courts. However, as I say, I should like to be enlightened by the House as to the general feeling regarding the regularity of the motion before pronouncing upon it.

Regarding
the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I beg to direct the attention of the House to the fact that the reference to the courts is of a specific character conveyed in the following words:
. Is section 17 of the Alberta Act in whole or m Pa.Il*' ultfa vires of the parliament of Canada, and if so in what particular or particulars?
. Now, my resolution is general in its bearing. The reference to the courts, as I say, is specific, referring solely to Alberta in relation to sction 17 of the Alberta Act. The present motion is general in its application in that it relates to the three prairie provinces, and that makes a decided difference.
I might call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that Premier Brownlee of Alberta has expressed himself on this question-and this, I submit, might be taken as an opinion bearing on the point of order-that the reference to the courts is entirely different from the question of the transfer of resources. On June 1 the government announced that they did not intend to proceed with the legislation promised in the speech from the throne at the opening of the session, but they kept that motion on the order paper and thereby prevented any discussion of the matter. So long as the government's motion remained on the order paper private 
members were precluded from introducing the subject. I repeat, my motion is general in its character, and it strikes me as subversive of democratic principles and of the liberties of members of the House that we should not be permitted to place on record our views on this important question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am sorry I had no intimation
that this matter would come up this afternoon, because I have not prepared for it. I would however refer you, Mr. Speaker, to May, thirteenth edition, at page 323:
Matters awaiting the adjudication of a court of law should not be brought forward in debate.
The same view is stated in Bourinot and of course in Beauchesne. All I have to say is that this question cannot be debated, at least in so far as the second part of it is concerned. As regards the first part of the resolution, as to the desirability of transferring Alberta's natural resources to the province. I think every one agrees on that point, because after all an agreement had been reached in the matter. That agreement, however, is subject to the qualification that it shall not interfere with, restrict or modify the right of the province to the complete control of its educational or other local affairs. That is where the disagreement comes in. I may add that an agreement has been entered into in that respect.
Had I known the matter would come up this afternoon I would have been prepared to refer the House to the statement I made last year, and which is in Hansard. However, I cannot debate the subject without referring to the very question which is submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada at the present time, and even if no rule existed to govern us in the matter I would not consider it proper, nor indeed would it be dignified on my part or on the part of any member of the House, to discuss a question which is actually pending before the Supreme Court of Canada. I think the motion is clearly out of order.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St George):
speechtext:
There is, I think, a dear distinction between the issue now before the Supreme Court of Canada and the issue raised in this resolution. This resolution proposes that it is in the general interest of this Dominion that their natural resources should be transferred to the prairie provinces. That has nothing to do with the question before the Supreme Court of Canada as to whether section 17 of the Alberta Constitutional Act

Natural Resources-Prairie Provinces
of 1905 is intra vires or ultra vires. The resolution then proceeds:
And that such transfer should not interfere with, restrict or modify the right of the said provinces to complete control of their educational or other local affairs.
The transfer itself will not interfere with the control of education. The contention underlying the reference to the Supreme Court of Canada is that the Constitutional Act of Alberta of 1905 and the similar Saskatchewan Act, 1905, affect the question of the use by these provinces of certain educational funds and educational grants, I may simply state that I think there is a clear distinction. Every person knows my view on this; I state frankly that I cannot support this resolution in the terms in which it is expressed; but I do think that, unless Your Honour regards it as clearly out of order, it is inexpedient and not in the public interest that questions which were discussed on every platform in my province during the last election and questions which are being discussed1 daily in the public press should not be debated in this House, in order that the public may be fully informed as to their general merits. As I have said, my views are well .known and I am prepared to stand in this House or in any other place and vindicate them, but I think it prejudicial to the interest of Canada and to the interests of this parliament that we should now prevent a discussion on a question which is of such general interest to the whole Dominion. I am sure that if ample discussion were allowed it would eliminate many misunderstandings which now exist with regard to the merits of the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does not my hon. friend think that the decision of the court as to the constitutionality of the act will clear things up better than a discussion in this House?

If my hon. friend will allow me to give him a frank answer, I will admit at once that a final decision on the issue placed before the court will decide as to whether or not, apart from this proposed transfer, certain restrictions placed upon the provinces with regard to the use of school funds are valid or not. To my mind, however, there is a clear distinction between a general term sulch as the transfer of natural resources to ithese several provinces and the transfer of the school funds and school lands. The term "natural resources", in its proper application, is a transfer to each of these provinces of those natural resources such as lands, mines and so on, which have not been appropriated under existing statutes. In regard to that transfer there is a subject for
discussion, in respect of which the maritime provinces and others have their own peculiar views.
Then with regard to these Dominion lands which have been set aside for school purposes in those provinces now comprising what were formerly the Northwest Territories, those lands have already been appropriated for the certain specific purposes, and already from the sale of those lands some 127,000,000 has accumulated, which amount is now held by the federal government in trust for educational purposes. Personally I do not think these school funds can be included, by any proper use of the words, in the natural resources of Alberta and Saskatchewan; I think that has been decided by parliament, and in respect of these school funds and school lands parliament is bound in honour to comply with the terms of the trust and to continue to administer it in accordance with those terms. Whether parliament shall decide that the crown in the right of the province or the crown in the right of the Dominion shall still continue to be trustee for these funds, my opinion is that the terms of the trust, whatever they may be, should be conserved.
What are the terms of the trust? It is true that a decision that section 17 of the Constitutional Acts of 1905 is ultra vires of parliament may, to a certain extent, modify the terms under which these funds are now held, and may affect to the same extent the terms by which they shall be held by the crown in the right of the province, in case that transfer is made. But apart from that one single issue there are broad questions which I am convinced, if discussed thoroughly in this House, would tend to remove many popular prejudices, sweep away a mass of misinformation now existing, and prove to be of great advantage not only to the government but to the whole of Canada.

Before Your Honour renders judgment I should like to direct attention to a matter that has a direct bearing upon the question whether or not the resolution is in order. The rule that my hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) has just referred to is of universal application. No high court of parliament should discuss a question that might prejudicially or otherwise, affect the interests of a litigant. That is the general rule. It therefore becomes necessary to inquire whether the reference to the Supreme Court of Canada is or is not litigation within the sense of the correct use of that word. In the Privy Council in 1912, in the case of the Attorney General for Ontario versus the Attorney General for Canada, it became necessary to determine whether or not the courts were bound to answer hypothetical questions thus submitted to them by the executive, and after a very full argument Lord Chancellor Earl Loreburn, in the course of his judgment, speaking for the commitee said this:
But the answers are only advisory and will have no more effect than the opinions of the law officers. Perhaps another reason is that the act has resulted in asking a series of searching questions very difficult to answer exhaustively and accurately without so many qualifications and reservations as to make the answers of little value. The Supreme court itself can, however, either point out in its answer the3e or other considerations of a like kind, or can make the necessary representations to the Governor General in Council when it thinks right so to treat any question that may be put.
Then these significant words appear at the close of the sentence:
And the parliament of Canada can control the action of the executive.

If that be so, it appears to me to be a very grave question whether or not this reference to the Supreme Court of Canada can be said to be litigation. That is the first difficulty which I have in this matter. The second difficulty which I have is this, that the Privy Council has said that the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada in answer to the questions submitted will be of no more importance than the opinion of the law officers of the crown, and inasmuch as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) signed the first agreement for the transfer of the resources, we must take it that his opinion was that there was no violation of fundamental rights under the constitution by reason of the agreement being made effective.
The matter now having been submitted by the executive to the court and the opinion of the court being no more valuable than that of the Minister of Justice, whose opinion has been already delivered inasmuch as he has signed the agreement, it seems to me to be somewhat difficult to say that this matter is now sub judice. If it were I would have no difficulty in arriving at the conclusion that it was out of order. But my difficulty at the moment is whether or not this can be said to be litigation or sub judice in the sense in which those words have been used in the various rules of parliament dating from the earliest days down to the present. If it is sub judice in the sense in which those words are used, I have no doubt that Your Honour should rule it out of order. But the significant words to which I have directed the attention of hon. members-
And the parliament of Canada can control the action of the executive.
-would make it quite possible for the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) to drop this resolution and move a resolution deprecating the reference of this question to the courts. Such a resolution would place at large the whole issue that is now being or about to be considered by the Supreme Court of Canada, inasmuch as the Privy Council has declared in the very terms I have used the right of this parliament to control the action of the executive.
I have the misfortune perhaps to differ from some of my colleagues with respect to one matter. I have no doubt the reference to the Supreme Court of Canada directly affects the question of the transfer of the resources for a reason that, I think, need only be stated to carry conviction. In the original agreement the transfer of the resources was

of course subject to the provisions of the Alberta act, and if the provisions of the Alberta act were intra vires, then obviously no further restrictions were necessary to preserve the rights of those who claim rights under its provisions on the school fund. But if on the other hand the provisions of the autonomy act, to which the transfer of the resources would be made subject, were ultra vires, it would follow that without restrictions or reservations the rights of minorities or majorities would be all the same and there would be no question with respect to the moneys under the school fund.
It is for that reason, I apprehend, that the matter has been referred to the Supreme Court of Canada; for, as the Minister of Justice has very properly said, if section 17 of the Alberta act is intra vires, by common consent, it seems to me, there is no further matter for its consideration or decision. But if on the other hand that section should be ultra vires, then clearly the question to be considered is what action, if any, should be taken by this parliament with respect to the matter that is mentioned in section 17. That is the whole question in a nutshell as I appreciate it at this moment.
I am one of those who perhaps differ again from some of my colleagues. I do not think it is desirable that we should discuss the question in parliament if it is sub judice in the sense that the question of the merits or demerits of special claims are to be considered. But if on the other hand we are merely to discuss the action of the executive in referring this matter to the courts instead of accepting the responsibility which the law imposes upon them, then another set of considerations should prevail.
I am free to say, Mr. Speaker, that my opinion is so hesitant with respect to this matter that I cannot render any assistance to you other than merely to point out the observations that were made with respect to what would result if the question were put to the Supreme Court of Canada, particularly having regard to the fact that the province of Alberta has indicated its intention not to be represented before the court at that hearing. Notice was given by a resolution that a bill would be introduced into parliament, at its present session, to approve and give effect to the said agreement as so modified, but a question having been raised as to the constitutional validity of section 17 of the Alberta Act, relative to the subject of education and schools within the said province, it was decided not to proceed with the proposed legislation as drafted until this question of doubt could be authoritatively settled.
The minister, therefore, recommends that the following question be referred by Your Excellency in Council to the Supreme Court, of Canada for hearing and consideration, pursuant to section 60 of the Supreme Court Act:-
Is section 17 of the Alberta act, in whole or in part, ultra vires of the parliament of Canada, and, if so, in what particular or particulars?
The committee concur in the foregoing recommendation and submit the same for approval.
That is the question referred to the Privy Council. Then the hon. member for Fron-tenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is in the general interest of this Dominion that their natural resources should be transferred to the prairie provinces at the earliest possible moment and that such transfer should not interfere with, restrict or modify the right of the said provinces to complete control of their educational or other local affairs.
There again are two questions, the question of the transfer of lands and the question of control of education. The hon. member stated

a moment ago that his motion as drafted was general in its terms, and concluded from that that as the other motion only affected one province and his motion dealt with the three prairie provinces, there was no analogy between the two cases. There is a good old rule of logic which says that the general includes the particular; there are only three prairie provinces, so what affects one with regard to the transfer of natural resources and educational powers affects the others unless there are special statutes governing 'the other provinces.
What do we find in Bourinot? At page 301 we have the following:
A matter which is under adjudication by a court of law cannot be brought before the House by motion or otherwise.
Bourinot does not state, as the leader of the opposition said a moment ago, that the matter before the court must be one which would affect an individual, in connection which any discussion might abridge or prejudice any rights he might have.
Bourinot makes no such distinction. Whether an individual or a collectivity of individuals is before the court, the case is not altered. The rule is that when a matter is under adjudication by a court of law, whether it affects an individual or a collectivity of individuals, whether it affects one man or one province, it cannot be brought before the House by motion or otherwise. In this connection May says, at page 323:
Matters awaiting the adjudication of a court of law should not be brought forward in debate. This rule was observed by Sir Robert Peel and Lord John Russell, both by the wording of the speech from the throne and by their procedure in the House regarding Mr. O'Connell's case, and has been maintained by rulings from the chair.
Redlich, at page 59 of volume 3, says:
Nothing has been done to weaken the force of another rule of a similar kind, that no reference must be made in debate to matters before the courts of law in some pending litigation.
And Beauchesne says, in par. 234 under rule 19:
Besides the prohibitions contained in this rule, it has been sanctioned by usage both in England and in Canada, that a member, while speaking, must not refer to any matter on which a judicial decision is pending.
The hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) referred a moment ago to past parliamentary experience. I remember a case in point which I am sure will be recalled by the leader of the opposition as well. Some years ago, after a Dominion census, the representation of the maritime provinces as well as that of Ontario was reduced, affecting the 
maritime provinces to a greater extent. That result raised a storm in the maritime provinces, because they felt rather aggrieved in view of that reduction. The matter was brought up in the House, and as a doubt was expressed with regard to the terms of the compact at the time of confederation, since which time the boundaries of Ontario and Quebec were enlarged and the other new provinces of the west came into existence, the govern' ment of the day decided to refer the matter to the Supreme court from where it went to the Privy Council. I had the honour to represent the Department of Justice in a minor capacity as Solicitor General and had with me as counsel Mr. Justice Newcombe and Air. Edward Blake. If I remember well, during the session of parliament, while the case was pending, a member representing one of the counties in the maritimes brought up the question in order to give vent to the grievances of his province. The point was raised that the matter was then pending before the courts, and that point of order was sustained. I cannot cite the exact dates, but the occurrence is quite within my memory, and that is a case in point.
Under these circumstances I must declare the present motion out of order, because it refers to a matter which is sub judice, awaiting adjudication before the courts of the land, and I so rule.

subtopic: PROPOSALS AS TO SUPPLY, TARIFF AND TOLLS
speechtext:
The subject of this resolution has been before the House now for six sessions. It urges the adoption of a national coal policy. It has never been possible to make any headway with the matter because we are so hemmed in by rules and regulations derived from the middle ages that it is practically impossible to make any headway in solving the economic problems of this country. What, we want at the present time is a Mussolini to try and solve some of these problems.
In my opinion we have the- most impractical form of government of any country in the civilized world. It is impossible to make any headway in Canada to solve economic problems and give relief. We have spent $2,000,000,000 on a national railway and a merchant marine, and to-day we are absolutely at the mercy of a foreign country for our fuel supplies. When every pound of coal we use can be mined and coked under the British flag, whether it be from Wales or the maritime provinces or Alberta, we have a ready market for United States coal foisted upon the people of this country by the directors of the Canadian National Railways who are entirely responsible for their failure to solve this problem.
I do not see the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) in the chamber to-day. He is the understudy, I might say, of the head of this system. After all is said and done, the coal question is 95 per cent a transportation problem, and after all these expenditures on a
[Mr. Church.1
national railway and a merchant marine we find that we might just as well own nothing when the question comes to solving any of the economic problems of the country.
The first clause of the resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the time has arrived for Canada to have a national poliey in relation to its coal supply and that no part of Canada should be left dependent on United States for such supply.
This principle has been adopted for six sessions by this House and nothing has been done by the government to give effect to it. The second clause reads:
That the government should immediately consider the initiation of an all British and Canadian coal supply, and that such a policy is both a social and economic necessity and in the best interests of the future of Canada.
This clause has been adopted now five or six times for this House and never carried out. The third clause reads:
That, the government should consider the advisability of placing a duty on coal from the United States to insure an all British supply for Canada and thus afford adequate protection to coal mined and coked under the British flag.
This clause of the resolution was adopted but never carried out. The only way in which this question can be solved is by adequate protection for coal mined in Alberta, the maritime provinces and Wales. The four native industries of Canada are the mining industry, the fisheries, agriculture and lumber, and they can be placed on their feet in this country only by a proper application of the gospel of protection, namely subsidies or subventions and bonuses. Although I come from the protectionist province of Ontario which votes Conservative, every time a resolution of this importance comes before the House we find that a large number of the members from that province absent themselves from the chamber. It is all very well to get up and support our national coal policy in the cities and towns of the province when the elections are on; but when they come to Ottawa-oh! what a difference to try and get action.
What is suggested in this resolution is that the principle of protection, subsidies, bonuses and subventions, should be applied to solve the problem of the coal industry in the maritime provinces and Alberta. The fourth clause of the resolution reads:
That, whereas coal is a necessity in effect equal to that of food, the government should consider the advisability of having it carried on a preferential toll basis by the railways on the same basis as grain and flour, and of granting subsidies and subventions to this industry.

National Cool Policy
This has been approved by two premiers, the premiers of Alberta and Ontario, and the problem will never be solved in any other way than by the gospel of protection. The United States could starve this country out of fuel in one winter. During a coal strike sve are absolutely at the mercy of the people of the United States for a pound of coal. During one of the coal strikes in that country, Canada was exhibited to the people of the United States as a Lazarus sitting around the coal sidings of the United States railways begging for a few lumps of coal. That was a humiliating position for the people of this country to be in, and after we have sipent $2,000,000,000 on railways we find the directors of the Canadian National Railways to-day folding their arms and saying that they will have practically nothing to do with the matter. If there were anything to test the size and ability of the Minister of Railways to administer his department it would be his ability to solve this matter which has been made a political football of by the directors of the national railways, by the railway commission, by the Minister of Railways and the government generally. This question has been referred to the railway commission. I am surprised that Your Honour has not ruled this motion out of order also on the ground that the question is before the judiciary. Any matter is not to be discussed here if sub judice before a police magistrate, a judge or court of record. The courts might as well take parliament's duties over. Is this a free parliament or is it not? Are we to sdt here like a lot of rubber stamps for the directors of the national railways and have our front benchers run out of the chamber whenever an economic question like this comes up for solution? What are we sitting here for? Why are we elected? Do the people or the courts or the railway commission rule in this country? A year ago the minister Said in this House that he would refer this question to the railway commission. What happened to the application? They made a political football out of dt. They killed a whole year's time. They declined to give a hearing until a week ago. The Premier of Ontario had lawyers before the commission for the past year, and the Premier of Alberta also had lawyers before the commission. A proper application had been made but the railway commission fell down. The government of this country should reorganize that commission in the public interest, so that whenever a reference is made by the high court of parliament a special sitting of that commission should be held a week after the reference is received and it should take precedence over
all other business. They should have heard the application of Ontario and Alberta and given a decision.
The national railways should agree to carry coal for $7 a ton. I am not criticising Sir Henry Thornton personally, but his action in coming over here and practically telling the people that, as regards the coal problem, they can stew in their own juice and that, so far as he is concerned, we can continue to buy coal in Alberta and pay the freight rate of $9 a ton. He might as well have said $22 a ton, because it would be just as prohibitive. The directors of the national railways are content that we should depend upon the United States and American coal barons for our coal supply They are willing to see Canada continue in the future as it has done in the past to be virtually a Lazarus sitting at the feet of the Pennsylvania railways and coal barons waiting for a few lumps of coal. You will never get this question solved as long as the present board of directors are in office, as long as the present Minister of Railways is in office or as long as the present railway commission is in office. The Minister of Railways to-day has all his powers taken away from him by legislation. He has practically no functions, no duties to perform except to act as an understudy for Sir Henry Thornton and the directors of the Canadian National Railways, to introduce what bills they hand to him and to administer the affairs of the Newmarket canal and the Trent canal. The great powers that were in the hands of the Minister of Railways in the past have been transferred to the railway commission,. The administration of the Intercolonial, the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the other railways, has been taken from him and handed! over to Sir Henry Thornton, and the board of directors of the national railways. The portfolio of railways, so far as any active-functions are concerned might just as well be abolished.
What did Mr. Carvell, the late chairman of the railway commission say? He said practically that he did not believe the railway commission had any jurisdiction in view of the new Canadian National Railways acts, over the component parts of the Canadian National Railways or over that system. It is no wonder that even some of the good Liberals and Liberal papers are getting tired. The Globe, George Brown's own paper, is a good Liberal paper and it has not deserted the Liberal party. It is the Liberal party that has deserted the principles of George Brown and the Globe. The Globe,
National Coal Policy

which for years was and is the backbone of the Liberal party in Ontario, had this to say last Saturday:
Trifling with the Coal Rates
It is a year since the order in council was passed calling for a hearing by the Dominion railway board on the question of freight rates on coal from Alberta to central Canada. When at last the case came up on Thursday it developed that the parties interested did not have necessarjr statistics prepared. Adjournment had to be taken until June 7. If at that time a favorable rate is granted, coal from the western mines cannot be moved east before February of next year, which means two years from the date of the order in council. Thus the ponderous machinery of rate investigation drags itself along.
Possibly it has not been forgotten that an insistent demand for Alberta coal arose in Ontario during the course of the United States anthracite strike, when a temporary rate of nine dollars a ton was allowed. This, the railway experts contended at the time, was an irreducible minimum. There was no doubt in their minds about it. Presumably they were speaking from knowledge of statistics. Both Alberta and Ontario disputed the figures, but the railwayman stood pat. Yet on Thursday representatives of both the C.P.R. and C.N.R. revealed the fact that they had no data available from which to present arguments, and that the necessary information could not be compiled in less than two months.
Did hon. members ever hear of such a thing, that in two years they were not able to compile the figures?
This looks pretty much like trifling with the whole question. Granted that the general freight rates question occupied much time, could not the railways have been prepared to meet the provincial representatives on Thursday if they were really anxious to do so? Are they of the opinion that delays and adjournments will push the coal question into the background until another strike brigs it to the fore? There seems no good reason for this, nor is there any reason for believing that the interested prov-vinees are going to let the matter drop until they know what it should cost to lay western coal down in this province. The consumers here want to know, and the dealers want to know'. If the cost is satisfactory it will be good business for the country to have this outlet for the Alberta product. Would it not be equally good business for the railways?
I say, Mr. Speaker, that the railway commission has allowed the two railways to trifle with the situation. For the past five or 3ix years we have had a select committee of the House endeavouring to deal with the situation. They took the evidence of experts, and made their report to the high court of parliament, which showed that the seven dollar rate or less was a fair one, and practically no objection was raised to it. Now here we have a railway on which two billion dollars were spent, and we have special trains and private cars running all over the country, and

thousands of cars sometimes empty at the head of the lakes in the slack season and we have very few cam operating between Alberta and Ontario to carry coal. Now, what is the position in Canada? The people of this country are looking for a Mussolini to arise in Canada and to solve some of our economic problems. I will read to the House what Mussolini has said:
My colleagues m the cabinet and the undersecretaries of states know that the government business must be handled with enthusiasm and promptitude. Our work must be intensive and productive. They know my requirements in this regard. They know that they cannot approach me unless their mission is one of government business. There is no time to joke. Everything must be to the point and must be worth discussing. Each usually has his business well-defined, and when he sees me, need stay but a few minutes. They have acquired skill in condensation which enables me to go quickly to the matter in hand and to settle it.
I am fortunately blessed with a faculty for quick decision which permits me to accomplish an immense amount of work. I cannot stand vacillating and procrastinating executives. Ministers of a professional type are useless as administrators. They take so much time for decision that the -whole business of their department is delayed. This cannot be tolerated in any branch of my government. Ministers, before we came into power, deliberated and vacillated for years before putting into operation. We have created an aptitude for quick decision in our public affairs which, coupled with our intensive efforts, has achieved things not dreamed of before our advent to power.
Another paragraph in his remarks reads as follows:
We have settled our debts with England and America, stiffened Italian finance, strengthened the lira and now have consolidated the public debt by the launching of the Lictoral loan. For our sea commerce we built the Roma, the biggest ship in the Mediterranean service, and will build two new liners, Rex and Dux, the fastest in the world, 40 knots an hour, taking only four to five days from Italy to New York and seven to Buenos Aires.
Fascism constructed in two years the Rome-Ostia electric line, a project planned for twenty years, designed to give the people of Rome access to their own seashore. Fascism constructed the Apulia aqueduct to supply forty communes with an -aggregate population of 3,000,000 with water; is building the longest tunnel in the world between Florence and Bologna-15 miles long-is completing the Rome to Naples direct line to reduce the running time by one-half, and undertaking numerous projects to be brought to successful consummation under Fascist initiative and drive.
He -goes on to point out:
Government, to be good, must be efficient. It must achieve the greatest net result with the minimum of lost effort. If there be wastage of labour, duplication, overlapping or lack of co-ordination, then there are serious defects in the government machinery. There must be unity of policy, unity of responsibility and

National Coal Policy
unity of direction. Without these, government becomes a slipshod, haphazard, hit-or-miss business, able to continue only because it can demand tribute from the entire nation.
A private business must be efficient or die. It has no reserve on which to call unless it has created that reserve itself. It must sustain itself by its own merits. Its manager must avoid wastage, duplication, overlapping and must co-ordinate all the parts of his organization in a smooth-running machine. He is responsible and held to strict account for its success. He directs it with a single aim and single policy, his policy.
That is what this country wants to-day- a modern Mussolini. We require efficient men to manage our railways. People have put their money into the country and into the railways, and we want a board of directors who will not build up Canada for Americans, but will build up the country for Canadians. I have criticised the board of directors of that railway and the Minister of Railways in regard to the management of the concern and their failure to carry out parliament's orders to initiate a national coal supply.
Then we have had a committee of this hon. House which took hundreds of pages of evidence on the coal question every session, and what have they done? Have the railway commission carried out the orders of parliament? Parliament has adopted a resolution on four or five different occasions for a national coal supply. Has the board of directors of the railway given effect to it? Has the railway commission carried it out? Have they done anything to jput in the seven dollar rate? No. They have carried grain and flour at a few cents a bushel, under the Crowsnest pass tolls, but when it comes to giving a rate for coal they decline to give it, and they make this question a political football. A day of reckoning to the railway commission is coming and also a day of reckoning for the board of directors of the Canadian National Railway.
I have here a letter from William Buchanan, a coal merchant of London. He has been reading statements in the press about the movement to establish coking plants for Canadian coal. He says that there are several coking plants in Canada, but very few of them are using their own coal. He also states that he is willing to put up a bond of $30,000 to guarantee the payment of all freight charges and the cost of all coal ordered from the province of Alberta. He says:
This coal would be bought and sold by me and I would guarantee the quality of same and also the service to be the very best.
He sold 5,000 tons of Alberta coal in the London district and says it is good material.
I observe my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) is present. He has taken an active part in this matter and I want to thank him and the representatives from Alberta for their assistance in this matter. I do not say it is the fault of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart). He had tried to do his part, but he has been handicapped, and by whom? By the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways. Sir Henry Thornton and his directors are content to have the people of this country hewers of wood and drawers of water for the Pennsylvania coal barons. The Canadian National Railways might as well have fixed twenty dollars a ton instead of nine, because nothing has been carried at the nine dollar rate lately.
I do not expect the government of to-day will do anything. They will do nothing. I have brought up this matter several times, and as long as I am in this chamber I will present the matter to parliament. The province of Ontario's application has been made a football of by the government. The Canadian National Railways have sold our merchant marine ships which cost a million and a half for a few thousand dollars. Many of these ships could be utilized for five months of the year. They could be converted into lake and ocean carriers. They could have brought coal from Wales as they brought it from the maritimes. They have brought 560,000 tons of coal from Wales and the maritimes this past season into the port of Montreal to save that port from a coal famine. I contend that if the board of directors of the National railways had any conception of their duty they would utilize those ships to bring coal past Montreal up to the head of the lakes. The national railways, in its turn, should have done its part to help the people of Alberta send their coal to Ontario and central Canada. The people of Ontario want Alberta coal. A united effort would result in mutual benefit to the people of both provinces. The Ontario government has had its representatives before the railway commission in.an attempt to get the commission to deal with the subject for a year. I think it is the duty of the Minister of Railways to instruct the chairman of that commission that they hold sittings forthwith from day to day to hear the evidence which has been taken before the coal committee of this House and find a solution for this particular problem.
I have almost given up hope of getting anything practical accomplished in this country. Notwithstanding our various legislatures we are not a practical people. I believe the Canadian people are the most impractical in
National Coal Policy

the world-except in time of war. You can mobilize the transportation system of the country in time of war. Why cannot you do it in time of peace? Simply because this parliament seems to have no jurisdiction over the president and management of the Canadian National Railways, who are in law and fact beyond our control evidently.
In solving this problem I think we can apply the principle of protection as did Mr. Stanley Baldwin to put the native industry of the old country on its feet. He applied there the principle of bonuses and subventions. I think a transportation rate of from $6 to S6.50 a ton in trainload1 lots should be given by the Canadian National railways. This should not be charged, or any part of it, to the provincial governments of Ontario and Alberta. This House very readily voted $35,000,000 to bondholders of the Grand Trunk Pacific without requiring them to prove their claims in the Exchequer court; we ignored the Exchequer court and the railway commission; but when it comes to giving a subvention of a few thousand dollars, oh my, what a difference 1
This is the case in a nutshell. Are the people of Canada after all these expenditures on railways and on our government merchant marine to be hewers of wood and drawers of water for the coal millionaires of Pennsylvania? You will never solve this problem until you take it out of the hands of the railway commission and Sir Henry Thornton and have parliament compel the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways to give a proper rate for the transportation of this particular commodity. Parliament should amend the Railway Act. There should be special rates granted for the movement of coal just as there are for the movement of grain and flour. I am glad that I have a new supporter for my views of the past six years in the person of the Premier of Ontario, Mr. Ferguson. I am very glad to have his support for the policy of protecting our four great basic industries-mining, lumbering, agriculture and fishing-and that they should be given preferential rates on our railways. This is not the first time that the railways have given preferential treatment to certain commodities. Notwithstanding what the Minister of Railways said the other night, I can prove every statement I have made. I proved everything last June before Sir Henry Thornton in the committee on railways and shipping.
The minister made statements the other night here which he cannot back up. I never referred to the Chateau; I did to the Vancouver hotel. I referred to special tolls and special rates on certain basic products. I 
challenge a searching inquiry into this whole railway. When the railway commission has fallen down it should be reorganized, and if the board of directors of the national railways cannot solve this problem, the sooner we have a new board of directors the better.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say that I am very much disappointed that nothing has been done in the past twelve months. Notwithstanding that this is the most important problem before us to-day we are just m the same position as we were two or three years ago.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a hardy
annual, and we are indebted to the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) for its periodical introduction. I think his resolution would have been better worded had he made it apply to the railway commission. A national coal policy is a very vital question, and I may point out to the House that the government has given it a great deal of thought and in 1922 appointed a board to study it. That board has been doing so almost continuously since that time with a view frankly to avoid the imposition of a duty, as suggested by my hon. friend. I may say that he did not hold that opinion at one time, as quotations from Hansard will show. It was felt, just as my hon. friend has stated, that as coal was as important as bread to the consumers of this country, no undue disability should be placed upon it to enhance its price. Not only that, but the most earnest advocates of the bringing of coal from Alberta have never asked that any subvention be applied towards the cost of its haulage, but rather that the real cost of the transportation of this commodity be ascertained and that a rate based on that cost be applied over the two railway systems, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National.
Now, as I say, we have made some study of the question, and my further remarks will diverge somewhat from the clear definition of the motion itself, nevertheless I think it important that they should be put on# Hansard for the information of every member of the

National Coal Policy
House of Commons who is interested in this question. For that purpose I have prepared the following statement:
In dealing with the question raised by the hon. member for Toronto Northwest, it is necessary that consideration be given to certain fundamental facts which more or less control the situation as it exists in Canada to-day. It is evident to all who have studied the political and economic geography of the world that nature has not distributed her resources in raw materials in such a way as to meet the needs of all the nations of the earth or to fully meet their economic requirements. That condition prevails in regard to food supplies, forest resources, mineral resources and all other raw materials. In other words, no nation is so bountifully provided by nature with all raw materials to the extent that she is entirely self-supporting and independent of all other nations.
The political boundaries of most countries were defined long ago; long before the demand for raw materials became as acute as it is to-day. These boundaries were defined to conform to physical features and on account of consideration of national defence rather than with the object of embracing supplies of those raw materials that have now become so essential to the economic life of a people. And when you get this more or less accidental location of international boundaries combined with the extremely sporadic distribution of raw materials you get a condition which is the cause of uneasiness and even alarm among those nations lacking certain essential resources.
We see this condition very well exemplified in the case of minerals. In all cases the distribution of mineral resources over the face of the earth is extremely erratic. In some cases the occurrence of important mineral supplies is so limited as to constitute natural national monopolies of that mineral.
Take the case of nickel-a highly important industrial metal. We find nickel1 only in Canada and in New Caledonia, but such a large share of the nickel resources lies in Canada that we practically have a national monopoly of that mineral. Chile had a monopoly on nitrate supplies until the discovery was made that nitrogen could be obtained from the air. Potash, another important mineral used as a fertilizer, occurs mainly in Germany and Alsace; asbestos in Canada and Rhodesia; mercury only in Spain, and so on.
When we come to coal supplies we find the conditions somewhat better, for nature has been more generous in distributing her coal resources over the face of the earth. Even in
this resource-one which is perhaps the most important of all mineral resources-we find this condition, namely, the United States with fifty per cent of the world supply, China with about thirteen per cent, Canada with about seventeen per cent and the whole of the rest of the world with the small balance remaining. We find also many countries, some of them highly developed industrially, with little or no coal resources at all. Norway, Sweden, Finland, several of the African and most of the South American countries have no coal resources at all and such countries as Italy, Spain -and other European countries are largely dependent upon outside sources of supply.
The result of this condition is that no country, with the exception of Great Britain and possibly Germany is wholly independent of foreign sources of coal supply. Even the United States with fifty per cent of the world supply imports a considerable quantity of coal from Canada into the northwestern states, and Australian coal is marketed in California. This condition, namely, the erratic distribution of coal fields is the root of the coal problem of Canada.
The question of how to overcome the irregular distribution of raw materials has been considered by the economists of many nations and has been raised and discussed by the League of Nations in Geneva. A committee of the league, after giving careful consideration to the various aspects of this situation, has come to the conclusion that the most feasible means of overcoming the disabilities under which various nations labour through lack of supplies of essential raw materials is by the ado'ption of complete free trade in all these materials. They recognize, however, the difficulties in the way of persuading all nations to adopt this policy, particularly those nations most favoured by nature with an abundance of these materials.
If we look at the coal situation of the world we find that three countries dominate the coal trade, namely, United States, Great Britain and Germany, because the great producing coalfields of the world are situated within their boundaries. They produce normally over 80 per cent of the total world production and, in addition to being the chief consuming countries, they are the countries having the largest exportable surplus. The chief deficit countries, on the other hand, are France, Italy, Holland, Switzerland, Austria, Spain and the Scandinivian countries on the east of the Atlantic; and Canada, Brazil, Argentine and other South American states on the other side. Of the exporting countries
National Coal Policy

Germany normally dominated the land trade of central Europe, while British coal controlled the maritime trade of the Atlantic, providing fuel for the countries- bordering the North Sea, Baltic, Mediterranean and the Atlantic coasts of Spain and Prance. A small trade is done with the Sputh American countries. United States sends the major portion of her exportable surplus to Canada and the remainder goes to Central and South America and only a small portion crosses the Atlantic, mainly to Italy.
Such are the broad features of coal production and movement in the world. If we were to go into the question of the zones controlled by the different producing fields we would find that the controlling factors for each field are:
(1)	Geographical location,
(2)	Cost of production, and
(3)	Quality of coal.
Governed by these factors each field under normal conditions of trade has its own recognized and fairly well defined market and this market is determined not by proximity to the coal field, but primarily by the cost of transportation, and only to a minor extent by political boundaries. Por example, under present freight rates, it costs no more to carry coal three thousand miles across the Atlantic than it does to transport it two hundred miles by rail over here. This is what gives Great Britain, whose coalfields are only a few milea from the sea, so much wider range for her coals than the United States whose coalfields are two hundred to four hundred miles from the sea. Fluctuation in costs of production, changes in transportation rates, or industrial disturbances, will cause some shifting of the zones controlled by each field, as was the case when American coal went to Great Britain during the strike of 1921 and again during the recent strike in 1926; and when British coal came to the United States in 1922. But unless substantial tariffs are applied against certain coals, political boundaries do not affect the shifting of the market zones.
A study of the coal trade of the world indicates clearly that except as it may be affected to a limited degree by tariff barriers, coal from each field moves freely into definite markets which are determined primarily by the cost of transportation, to some extent by cost of mining and the quality of coal, but only slightly by political boundaries.
An appreciation of this fact makes it easy to understand why we are importing coal from a foreign country when we have an abundance of our own. It is one of the

consequences of the uneven distribution of the natural resources of the earth and of laying out political boundaries in defiance of natural conditions.
An inspection o-f the -tariffs of the three largest coal-producing countries of the world shows that they place coal in the duty-free list. In the case of Great Britain and Germany there is no import duty on coal, and in the United States coal is in the dutyfree list, but with a proviso that on coal coming from any country which levies a duty on United States coal an equal duty will be levied on coal imported into the United States from such country. For example, United States duty on Canadian coal is determined by the duty which Canada imposes on United States coal.
Although France is a deficit country as regards coal requirements there are in that country important coal mining industries. The French tariff of 1910, which is the basic tariff still in force, imposed a duty of 12 centimes per hundred kilogrammes on coal. With the exchange value of the franc at 19.3 cents Canadian money, which was its value in 1910, this was equivalent to about 25 cents Canadian money per metric ton of 2,240 pounds. The original rate of 12 centimes is now increased by a co-efficient of 1.7 making 20.4 centimes. With the franc at its present exchange value of four cents this is the equivalent of about eight cents per metric ton.
An instance of a high tariff on coal is found in Spain, a country whose coal requirements are not large. In the Spanish first tariff-higher tariff-there is a duty of 22.50 pesetas per metric ton on all grades of coal. The corresponding rate under the second tariff is 7.50 pesetas. These are gold pesetas. The equivalent in Canadian money per metric -ton would be about $4.35 first tariff, and $1.45 second tariff. There is a conventional rate to England of four pesetas per metric ton on pit coal, that is, about 73 cents.
Italy, a fairly large importer of coal, imposes no duty. In Canada we admit anthracite, lignite and coke free of duty. The general tariff on bituminous coal, all grades, imposes an import duty of 50 cents per net ton. On bituminous coal imported for the manufacture of coke by operators of by-product coke ovens, a rebate of 99 per cent of the duty is allowed. Under the provisions of the British preferential tariff bituminous coal coming to Canada direct from those British countries or possessions admitted to the benefit of the British

National Coal Policy
preferential tariff in Canada, is subject to an import duty of 35 cents per net ton. The intermediate tariff, which is a conventional tariff, provides for a duty of 45 cents per net ton on bituminous coal coming from countries to which the benefits of such intermediate tariff shall have been extended. Very little, if any, coal enters Canada under the provisions of this tariff.
A study of the underlying fundamentals of Canada's fuel problem takes us back a considerable number of years to the time when American anthracite was in the initial stages of being established as a staple household fuel in certain parts of Canada. A? far back as 1880 we find that Canada was importing half a million tons a year of this coal. Although it was probably not recognized at that time that the seeds of an acute fuel problem had been sown, subsequent events prove that such was the case. As our population increased, importations of American anthracite mto the cities and towns of central Canada had corresponding growth. The furnace equipment installed in the homes was adapted to the use of this coal, and considering the high degree of efficiency of anthracite as a household fuel, particularly when a better quality was coming into Canada than is the case to-day, it was only natural that the people using it became prejudiced in its favour. A large percentage of the population did so to the extent of believing it to be the only suitable fuel available for warming the home. The situation developed into one of dependency upon a single source of supply, and to accentuate the position this was a monopolistic source in a foreign country, although a very friendly one.
The coal strike in the United States coai fields in 1902-03 when supplies to Canada were interrupted was a serious warning to us of the precariousness of our fuel position. Then there were intermittent interruptions, though lesse serious, owing to freight embargoes and other transportation tie-ups in the United States, but it was the strike in the anthracite fields in 1922, synchronizing as it did with the railway shopmen's strike, that was the event that brought us to a true realization of our position. As an additional incentive for us to seek fuels that would replace American anthracite, unofficial intimation had been received from the United States Bureau of Mines that owing to the limited life of the Pennsylvania anthracite fields, Canada would have to work out her own solution for replacing the anthracite now imported from the United States. In recent years several bills have been introduced before the United States congress advocating an embargo on the export of anthracite to Canada. These did not pass, but they were an indication of growing uneasiness over the anthracite supplies in the United States.
Those were the events, in summary, which aroused publie attention to the extent of making the subject one of national interest and which prompted the government to institute action leading to a sustained effoi-t to satisfactorily solve this fuel problem.
We 'have also, in connection with our own coal mining industry, a number of problems relating to the industrial situation and to the distribution of Canadian coal. Some of these, however, are of local importance while others must be met and solved by the industry itself.
The coal industry of Vancouver island, for example, is faced with a problem brought about by the competition of cheap fuel oil from California, Mexico and Peru.
Alberta's problem is to extend her markets to absorb the production she is capable of making and so permit of more uniform production throughout the year. The capacity of her mines is estimated to be from ten to twelve million tons per year, while her present markets will absorb only about six million tons. It appears as if Alberta will have this problem with her always because of her enormous resources and the ease with which new mines can be opened. She will be constantly striving to secure new markets for the production she is capable of making unless steps are taken to prevent the opening up of new mines that are not necessary to supply existing demand. This is a problem arising out of a superabundance of coal resources. The provincial government has already met, with distinct success in extending the markets for Alberta coal.
In Saskatchewan there is the problem of the utilization of the great lignite beds.
In New Brunswick the industry is faced with a problem of how best to mine their thin seams and make the greatest possible recovery.
In Nova Scotia there are problems of markets, of submarine mining and of adjusting production to meet present and potential demands of our eastern provinces. These are some of the internal problems with which we are faced, and in striving for a solution we naturally look first to the underlying causes.
As a part of the process generally termed fluctuation in the realms of trade there is a constant succession of action and reaction. Periods of prosperity, with business expansion and rising prices, are followed by periods of depression with falling prices and deflation of
National Coal Policy

business. Abnormal demands for all sorts of manufactured goods arise at times, and manufacturing plants are enlarged to meet these peak conditions. Consequently when a reaction sets in and the demand falls off we have to face conditions of over production and the resultant unemployment in industrial areas.
The coal mining industry, as well as industries having to do with manufactured commodities, does not escape the penalties following conditions of over-production. In the case of our coal mining industries in Canada, however, over-development of the mines and capacity to produce far in excess of normal market requirements cannot in all respects be attributed to the rise and fall of the trade barometer.
In the case of Alberta the ease with which new mines can be opened has been one of the chief causes of over-development. An inspection of figures relating to the number of mines opened, and abandonments, will show that nearly two-thirds of the mines have been abandoned.
In the bituminous field over-development as regards number of mines is not so great, but the aggregate present capacity is about double the maximum output yet achieved. In this field there seems less danger in opening new mines because of the great expense involved.
In the sub-bituminous mines the number of operating units is likewise not great, and the rated capacity of these mines on the basis of 150 days operation per year does not show a very great excess over the output achieved, but on a full year of 300 days operation the output would, like that of the bituminous mines, be more than double.
In the lignite field, the over capacity of the present mines on a full year basis is between two and two and a half times the market requirements. It is in the lignite field that the over-development in numbers rather than in capacity is such a marked feature. Under the present system of marketing the lignite mines supplying the domestic trade are subject to sharp peaks of demand, and for a few weeks during the winter season work to capacity. This condition seems to be caused by the dealer and consumer buying only for immediate needs. Although such a system as this obviates the necessity for stocking coal and may be in itself an economical method of distribution, the apparent advantages are offset by too many disadvantages to the coal mining industry of the province.
In the case of Nova Scotia, over-capacity of the mines as relates to present market requirements is largely attributable to a set of unusual circumstances arising in connection

with the Great war. In the years 1912 and 1913 before the extra demands of the war had appeared Nova Scotia coal mines were producing from seven and three-quarter million to eight million tons of coal per annum. But in 1917 when there was a greatly increased demand for coal throughout the world, production in Nova Scotia had fallen off to about six and a half million tons. This was mainly due to labour shortage occasioned by the absence of so many miners who had enlisted for overseas service. Among these men were many skilled miners who occupied key positions in the mines and whose positions could not be filled. As a consequence of this and on account of ships being requisitioned for transatlantic service, a large part of the St. Lawrence trade was lost.
I w'ish to pass on now to what is the apparent cost of replacing United States coal, if I may do so without tiring the House. Over the years 1923-24-25 the average annual importations of American anthracite into the maritime provinces, the Quebec city district and Montreal district aggregated 1,276,425 tons. It is estimated that this imported coal could be replaced by British anthracite and coke manufactured from maritime province coals, provided that a market could be found for the surplus gas which is the most important by-product of the coking process. This replacement would absorb the surplus British anthracite accruing from our estimated importation of 600,000 tons, and would draw on maritime province coal production to the extent of 1,465,000 tons of coal.
Having regard to the normal consumption of maritime province coal, this extra tonnage for coking purposes would be applied to the surplus coming from the estimated 10,000,000 ton production. On this basis, therefore, and after dealing with the domestic requirements of the maritime provinces, Quebec city and Montreal districts, there would still be a surplus of 2,700,000 tons of maritime coal to be applied elsewhere.
Coking plants already in existence in Ontario and Quebec are importing about 1,500,000 tons annually of coking coal from the United States, and supplies to these plants would have to be allocated from the surplus of
2,700,000	tons of maritime coal, leaving 1,200,000 tons as a remainder.
Giving consideration to the fact that the extra production from the maritime province mines must necessarily be nearly all suitable for the manufacture of domestic coke, this remainder of 1,200,000 tons will be applied against replacement of some 200,000 tons of United States industrial coal imported into

National Coal Policy
the maritime provinces, 227,000 tons imported into the Quebec district and about 2,000,000 tons imported into the Montreal district. Together with 1,000,000 tons of British bituminous coal, the balance from the maritime provinces would fall short of filling these requirements by about 280,000 tons, which means that the discrepancy would have to be made up by bringing that amount of Alberta industrial coal to Montreal.
Now, the significance of this distribution of supplies is that, apart from the maritime province coals allocated to coking plants in Ontario, there would be no supplies of maritime coal available for the districts west of Montreal. It may be taken, therefore, that Alberta coal would be required for both domestic and industrial requirements in the area from Ottawa to the head of the lakes. In arriving at figures showing the cost of this replacement scheme, the calculation has been based upon a selling price of coke as 82 per ton less than that of anthracite, and also that notwithstanding an increase in the tariff to the point of excluding United States coals, the prices of Canadian coals in eastern Canada would not rise above normal market levels. Provided that such would be the case, the replacement of United States coal in the maritime provinces, the Quebec city district and Montreal district would effect a saving to the public of $1,300,000.

Extra cost to the public would likewise result in the other districts comprised of Ottawa, Kingston, North Bay, Windsor, Sault Ste. Marie and head of the lakes the aggregate of the extra cost amounting to $32,000,000. Summing up the
total cost of replacement, the net result is an annual extra cost to the public of $56,000,000. There would also be an annual loss in customs revenue amounting to $7,000,000. While this would be a high price indeed to levy on the coal-consuming public, let us consider what would be the advantages by way of compensation.
It is easy to appreciate the advantages that would be derived from a complete rehabilitation of the coal mining industry in the maritime provinces. The greatly increased production which would probably result in the mines working to capacity throughout the year would be of utmost importance to the industry, and indeed to the other lines of trade in those provinces. Increased demands of the St. Lawrence markets, particularly for coking coals, would remove many of the contentious issues that are now connected with banking and disposal of slack coal. A plan which would make it practicable to mine and bank coal in the winter for transportation by water during the season of navigation would be the means of overcoming the problem of unemployment during the winter months, and a difficulty in the Nova Scotia fields is to keep winter employment regular.
The advantages to the coal mining industry in the maritimes could be summed up under the statement that there would not only be a complete rehabilitation of the industry in those provinces, but it would probably enjoy a prosperity greater than has been the case in its history. The coal mining industry in Alberta would likewise benefit. The mines producing domestic coal would send down to Ontario nearly three and a half million tons annually, which would represent an increase of about one hundred per cent in the present combined production of the lignite and sub-bituminous mines. The bituminous coal fields would send down about ten million tons which would represent an output nearly three times that of the highest yearly total yet achieved. As the rated capacity of the Alberta bituminous mines is about double the present output, this greatly increased demand would probably necessitate the opening of new bituminous mines.
Unemployment periods in Alberta coal fields are perhaps subject to as much if not mors frequency than is the case in the maritimes. The great number of mines in operation and peak demands for coal are the very essence of unemployment periods, as well as tending to high cost of production. While it is recognized that there would be difficulties connected with the steady transportation of coal over the long haul to Ontario throughout all seasons
National Coal Policy

of the year, the stimulus to conditions in Alberta should put the industry on a well sustained basis.
Then there is consideration of the advantage to be derived from the annual diversion of some $75,000,000 or $80,000,000 from United States to Canadian channels of trade, the advantage being in connection with keeping this money in circulation within our own country rather than sending it abroad. Also, we have frequently heard expression of advantages that would accrue from the transfer of the source of supply of a large part of our coal requirements, from the United States to our own coal resources within the Dominion. The contention has been that such a procedure would remove our dependency upon neighbourly goodwill and the uncertainty of industrial peace in the United States coal fields. While in itself this would appear to be a desirable condition, another view can be taken of the situation; one that has to do with the conservation of our natural resources. Even allowing for the immensity of our coal resources, we are perhaps a little prone to measure the value of such things in terms of our own lifetime. Recent developments in low temperature carbonization processes indicate immense possibilities for the utilization of coal in the recovery of motor fuels and oils. In the face of the enormous and increasing consumption of petroleum products together with the rapid exploitation of the world's known oil reserves, the day when we shall turn to coal to supply our oil requirements may be nearer at hand than is readily appreciated. In the meanwhile Canada is not dependent upon the United States nor upon any other country as regards actual coal supplies. Our importations of coal are for economic reasons.
Probably the greatest disadvantage that would result from the institution of this replacement policy would be the annual levy of some fifty-six million dollars owing to increased price of coal to the consuming areas in central Canada. First of all we must consider what amount the tariff must be raised in order to exclude United States coal. It has been demonstrated that Ontario would have to bring coal from Alberta, and that the cost of industrial coal from Alberta would be $10.75 or $11 per ton laid down in Ontario, as against $5 to $7 American coal, and the bulk of the sales of American coal are closer to the $5 figure. The import duty on industrial coal, therefore, would have to be raised to approximately $6 per ton. The lowest effective duty on foreign anthracite and coke would probably have to be finally determined by

experiment stages. Based on the freight rate mentioned, I may say that I did not include that freight rate. This calculation is based on a $7 freight rate from Alberta. The information will, however, appear in the report; I was unable to take the time to incorporate it in my statement to-day.

The major portion of the burden of the price increase on industrial coal would fall on the railways. The Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways are together using about 3,800,000 tons of United States coal per year, most of which is consumed on locomotives operating in central Canada.
The steel industry in Canada has to meet severe competition from other countries. A higher cost of coal or its derivative coke, would tend to increase the difficulties of meeting this competition in the case of steel companies who are not proprietors of coal supplies.
Generally, the increased cost of industrial coal would increase cost of production of manufactured goods wherein coal is used in the manufacturing process. This would probably be productive of a movement for more protection for the manufacturing industries, and hence a cycle of tariff revision.
In seeking remedial measures for the domestic fuel situation, the Dominion fuel board has encouraged the introduction of a variety of competitive fuels for supplying the needs of central Canada, the object being to secure a surety of supply at reasonable prices. In these coalless areas of central Canada, the only natural fuel, apart from the wood fuel resources, is found in the peat bogs. These peat areas are very extensive and although the use of peat has not achieved much commercial success up to the present time, the fuel board is convinced of the future importance of this fuel as a substitute for coal during the fall and spring months, but the board does not recommend it as a substitute for coal during the severe winter months.
With the permission of the House I will lay on the table a copy of this report, which is very comprehensive, covering the fuel situation in Canada. It does not advocate the imposition of a duty. It does not advocate the payment of bounties or subsidies to the railways. It recommends simply the development of a reasonably national policy. The report goes on to show that we have in a very large way reduced importations! from outside and foreign fields for our coal supply. For example, in 1923 we were importing 5,000,000 tons of anthracite. In 1925 we imported just about 3,000,000 tons or a reduction of 2,000,000 tons. Therefore I say 'that we are in a very large way rapidly developing a national coal policy in Canada.
